questions.title: Effect of glucuronic acid conjugation on a drug
questions.question: The addition of glucuronic acid to a drug:

options.A: Usually leads to inactivation of the drug
options.B: Is an example of a Phase I reaction
options.C: Occurs at the same rate in adults and newborns

explanations.A: Correct. Glucuronidation (conjugation with glucuronic acid) is a Phase II metabolic reaction, and Phase II conjugation reactions typically inactivate a drug by attaching a large, polar group that abolishes its pharmacological activity. That same conjugation also increases the drug's water solubility, preparing it for renal excretion.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Glucuronidation is a Phase II reaction (conjugation), not Phase I -- Phase I reactions instead expose or add a reactive functional group by oxidation, reduction or hydrolysis, which typically precedes conjugation rather than being conjugation itself.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Glucuronide conjugation is markedly slower in newborns than in adults, because the neonatal liver has immature glucuronyl transferase activity. This is why neonates are especially vulnerable to toxicity from drugs cleared mainly by glucuronidation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Conjugation with glucuronic acid increases, not decreases, a drug's water solubility. That increase in polarity is exactly what allows the kidney to excrete the conjugated metabolite.

questions.subtopic: Phase I and Phase II metabolism
questions.learning_objective: State that glucuronidation is a Phase II reaction that inactivates a drug and increases its water solubility, and that it is slower in newborns than adults.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Usually leads to inactivation of the drug."

questions.title: What liver enzyme inducers increase the effect of
questions.question: Liver enzyme inducers increase the effect of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Enzyme induction speeds up metabolism, and for an ordinary active drug cleared by that pathway, faster metabolism means a reduced, not increased, effect. Being lipid-soluble does not, by itself, make a drug an exception to that.
explanations.B: Correct. A prodrug is inactive as administered and only becomes pharmacologically active after metabolic conversion. Enzyme induction speeds up the very reaction that generates the active drug, increasing rather than reducing its effect -- the one situation where faster metabolism raises, rather than lowers, a drug's action.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Enzyme induction reduces the effect of most ordinary drugs by clearing them faster, so "all drugs" is wrong. Prodrugs are the exception to that pattern, not the rule.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Enzyme induction does not selectively target water-soluble drugs. Induction's characteristic clinically relevant effect is on prodrug activation and on ordinary active drugs' clearance, not specifically on water-soluble drugs as a class.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that enzyme induction increases a prodrug's effect by speeding its conversion to active drug, unlike its usual dampening effect on ordinary drugs.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Prodrugs"
field_notes.pendingConcept: CON-FND-450B67836EBF1A is pending in docs/Kasr-Source-Imports/concept/108-INT-concepts-pharmacology.md, canonical_key teaching.pharma.metabolism.induction-inhibition -- applies only after Omar imports that Kasr batch

questions.title: A drug unlikely to reduce oral contraceptive effectiveness
questions.question: A woman is taking oral contraceptives (OCs). Which of the following drugs is unlikely to reduce the effectiveness of the OCs?

explanations.A: This DOES reduce OC effectiveness, so it is not the answer. Rifampin is a potent enzyme inducer, and inducers speed up OC hormone metabolism, lowering circulating hormone levels.
explanations.B: Correct. Ketoconazole is an enzyme INHIBITOR (of CYP3A4), not an inducer -- inhibition slows drug metabolism rather than speeding it up. It therefore does not accelerate OC hormone clearance, unlike the four enzyme-inducing anticonvulsants/antibiotics listed as the other options, making it the drug unlikely to reduce OC effectiveness.
explanations.C: This DOES reduce OC effectiveness, so it is not the answer. Phenobarbital is a classic hepatic enzyme inducer, and by speeding up OC metabolism it lowers circulating hormone levels.
explanations.D: This DOES reduce OC effectiveness, so it is not the answer. Carbamazepine is an enzyme inducer, and by the same mechanism as phenobarbital and rifampin, it speeds OC metabolism.
explanations.E: This DOES reduce OC effectiveness, so it is not the answer. Phenytoin is an enzyme inducer, and by the same mechanism as the other anticonvulsants/antibiotics listed, it speeds OC metabolism.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish an enzyme inhibitor (ketoconazole, which does not reduce OC effectiveness) from enzyme inducers (rifampin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine, phenytoin, which do).

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Ketoconazole"

questions.title: The main organ of drug metabolism
questions.question: The main organ which is responsible for drug metabolism is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lung does metabolise some drugs, as one of several extrahepatic sites, but it is not the main site of drug metabolism in the body.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The kidney is chiefly an organ of drug excretion. It does carry out a small amount of drug metabolism, but that is not its principal role.
explanations.C: Correct. The liver is the main site of drug metabolism, because of its rich supply of both microsomal and non-microsomal metabolising enzymes. Most orally absorbed drugs also pass through the liver first, via the portal circulation, before reaching the rest of the body.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The gut wall does contribute some first-pass metabolism for certain drugs, but it is not the main site of drug metabolism overall -- that role belongs to the liver.

questions.learning_objective: State the liver as the main site of drug metabolism, distinct from lesser extrahepatic sites.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Liver"

questions.title: What biotransformation usually leads to
questions.question: Biotransformation usually leads to:

options.A: Increase in the lipid solubility of the drug
options.B: Decrease in water solubility of the drug
options.C: Decrease in the lipid solubility of the drug
options.D: Increase in the activity of all drugs

explanations.A: Incorrect. Biotransformation generally moves a drug in the opposite direction -- toward lower, not higher, lipid solubility -- so that the kidney can eventually excrete it.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Biotransformation generally increases, not decreases, a drug's water solubility, since a more water-soluble metabolite is more readily filtered and excreted by the kidney.
explanations.C: Correct. The overall purpose of biotransformation is to convert a lipid-soluble drug, which would otherwise be reabsorbed indefinitely in the renal tubule, into a more polar, water-soluble metabolite the kidney can excrete. So biotransformation usually decreases lipid solubility.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Biotransformation frequently inactivates a drug, particularly through Phase II conjugation, and even Phase I reactions do not increase the activity of every drug. Some Phase I products are inactive, so "all drugs" is too absolute to be correct.

questions.subtopic: Phase I and Phase II metabolism
questions.learning_objective: State that biotransformation generally decreases a drug's lipid solubility to enable renal excretion.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Decrease in the lipid solubility of the drug"
field_notes.pendingConcept: CON-FND-44B6AE3E7DDA55, same pending Kasr 108-INT concept as Q095 above -- applies only after that batch is live

questions.title: What Phase I reactions do not include
questions.question: Phase I reaction includes all the following types of reactions except:

explanations.A: This IS a Phase I reaction type, so it is not the exception being asked for. Oxidation is one of the three classic Phase I reaction types, exposing or adding a reactive functional group to the drug.
explanations.B: This IS a Phase I reaction type, so it is not the exception being asked for. Reduction is one of the three classic Phase I reaction types.
explanations.C: This IS a Phase I reaction type, so it is not the exception being asked for. Hydrolysis is one of the three classic Phase I reaction types.
explanations.D: Correct -- this is the exception. Conjugation is a Phase II reaction, not Phase I. Phase I reactions expose or add a reactive group (oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis), while Phase II instead attaches a large polar group to that reactive site, and the drug typically leaves the body only after this second step.

questions.subtopic: Phase I and Phase II metabolism
questions.learning_objective: Classify oxidation, reduction and hydrolysis as Phase I reactions and conjugation as Phase II.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Conjugation"

questions.title: Effect of charcoal-broiled foods on drug metabolism
questions.question: Charcoal broiled foods may cause:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Charcoal-broiled food is a classic dietary inducer specifically of CYP-450 1A (via polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons produced by broiling), not of the 3A subfamily.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Charcoal-broiled food induces, rather than inhibits, this enzyme -- inhibition is the opposite direction of effect from what it actually causes.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Charcoal-broiled food's effect is induction, not inhibition, and it targets CYP-450 1A specifically, not the 3A subfamily.
explanations.D: Correct. Polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons produced by charcoal broiling are well-recognised dietary inducers of the hepatic CYP-450 1A enzyme subfamily. This speeds the metabolism of any drug cleared through that specific pathway, an example of a dietary, not pharmacological, cause of enzyme induction.

questions.learning_objective: State charcoal-broiled food as a dietary inducer of CYP-450 1A specifically.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Induction of CYP-450 1A"
field_notes.pendingConcept: CON-FND-450B67836EBF1A, same pending Kasr 108-INT concept as Q096 above -- applies only after that batch is live

questions.title: Risk for slow drug metabolizers
questions.question: Slow metabolizers are more liable to:

options.B: Failure to reach to the therapeutic effective levels

explanations.A: Correct. A slow metabolizer clears a drug more slowly than the average patient, often from a genetic polymorphism in a metabolising enzyme. A standard dose given at the usual interval therefore accumulates to higher-than-expected plasma levels over repeated dosing, raising the risk of toxicity.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Failing to reach therapeutic levels describes a FAST, not slow, metabolizer -- rapid clearance would leave plasma levels too low, the opposite problem from slow metabolism.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Therapeutic failure is again more characteristic of unusually rapid metabolism clearing the drug before it can act, not of slow metabolism, which instead causes the drug to build up.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Slow drug metabolism is a hepatic/enzymatic phenomenon; it is not, by this mechanism, a cause of renal failure.

questions.learning_objective: State drug accumulation as the characteristic risk in a slow metabolizer, distinct from the therapeutic-failure risk of a fast metabolizer.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Drug accumulation"
field_notes.pendingConcept: CON-FND-44B6AE3E7DDA55, same pending Kasr 108-INT concept as Q095 above -- applies only after that batch is live

questions.title: What enterohepatic circulation requires
questions.question: Enterohepatic circulation occurs with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. "All of the above" cannot be correct, because the other options are not all true -- enterohepatic circulation is specific to drugs excreted in bile, not to every route or drug type listed.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Enterohepatic circulation depends on biliary, not urinary, excretion -- a drug excreted in urine does not pass through the bile-gut-reabsorption loop that defines this phenomenon.
explanations.C: Correct. Enterohepatic circulation occurs when a drug or its conjugate is excreted into the bile, delivered to the intestine, and then partly reabsorbed back into the portal circulation instead of being eliminated in the faeces. This cycle prolongs the drug's presence in the body and is only possible for drugs excreted via bile.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Being water-soluble is not, by itself, what causes enterohepatic circulation -- the defining requirement is biliary excretion followed by intestinal reabsorption, not water solubility alone.

questions.learning_objective: State that enterohepatic circulation requires biliary excretion of a drug followed by intestinal reabsorption.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Drugs excreted in bile"

questions.title: Phase II reaction with a genetic polymorphism
questions.question: Which of the following is a phase II drug metabolism reaction associated with a genetic polymorphism?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Glutathione conjugation is a genuine Phase II reaction, but the reaction classically associated with a well-known genetic polymorphism (fast versus slow status) is acetylation, not glutathione conjugation.
explanations.B: Correct. Acetylation, via N-acetyltransferase, shows a well-documented genetic polymorphism: individuals are classified as fast or slow acetylators. This polymorphism has real clinical consequences, such as slow acetylators being more prone to isoniazid-induced peripheral neuropathy and drug-induced lupus.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Oxidation is a Phase I, not a Phase II, reaction, so it does not answer a question specifically about a Phase II reaction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Reduction is a Phase I, not a Phase II, reaction.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Glucuronidation is a genuine Phase II reaction, but it is not the reaction classically taught as showing the fast/slow genetic polymorphism -- that distinction belongs to acetylation.

questions.subtopic: Phase I and Phase II metabolism
questions.learning_objective: Identify acetylation as the Phase II reaction with a well-known fast/slow genetic polymorphism.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Acetylation"

questions.title: What does not cause oral contraceptive failure
questions.question: Failure of oral contraceptive pills may occur due to all the following EXCEPT:

options.C: The use of broad spectrum antibiotics as ampicillin

explanations.A: Correct -- this is the exception. Cimetidine is an enzyme INHIBITOR, not an inducer, so it slows rather than speeds OC hormone metabolism. That is the opposite mechanism from the inducers and absorption-reducing causes listed in the other three options, so cimetidine does not cause OC failure.
explanations.B: This DOES cause OC failure, so it is not the exception. Malabsorption reduces the amount of hormone actually absorbed, lowering circulating levels below the contraceptive threshold.
explanations.C: This DOES cause OC failure, so it is not the exception. Broad-spectrum antibiotics such as ampicillin can disrupt the gut flora that normally allows reabsorption of oestrogen during enterohepatic circulation, reducing circulating hormone.
explanations.D: This DOES cause OC failure, so it is not the exception. Phenytoin is an enzyme inducer, and by speeding OC hormone metabolism it lowers circulating levels.

questions.learning_objective: Identify cimetidine as an enzyme inhibitor that does not reduce OC effectiveness, unlike the enzyme-inducing and absorption-reducing causes of OC failure.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: The use of cimetidine"

questions.title: Urine pH manipulation and drug excretion
questions.question: One is true regarding drug excretion:

options.A: NaHCO3 decreases ionization of aspirin, so increase its excretion
options.B: NaHCO3 decreases ionization of atropine, so increase its excretion
options.C: Ammonium chloride increases ionization of morphine, so increase its excretion
options.D: Vitamin C increases ionization of aspirin, so increase its excretion

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sodium bicarbonate alkalinises the urine, which INCREASES, not decreases, the ionisation of aspirin, a weak acid. The more-ionised drug is trapped in the urine and excreted faster, so this option reverses the direction of ionisation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Atropine is a weak base, and alkalinising the urine with bicarbonate would DECREASE its ionisation, favouring reabsorption rather than excretion -- this option both mismatches the drug's ionisable character and reverses the expected effect.
explanations.C: Correct. Morphine is a weak base, and ammonium chloride acidifies the urine. In an acidic environment a weak base ionises more, and the ionised form cannot be reabsorbed across the renal tubule, so it is trapped in the urine and excreted faster -- the standard ion-trapping principle applied to accelerate elimination of a basic drug.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Vitamin C acidifies the urine, which would DECREASE, not increase, the ionisation of aspirin, a weak acid that ionises more in alkaline rather than acidic urine -- this option reverses the expected direction of the pH-ionisation relationship.

questions.subtopic: Ion trapping and urine pH manipulation
questions.learning_objective: Apply the ion-trapping principle to predict that acidifying urine (ammonium chloride) speeds excretion of a weak base (morphine), and correctly pair weak-acid/weak-base drugs with the urine pH change that traps them.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Ammonium chloride increases ionization of morphine, so increase its excretion"

questions.title: Volume of distribution and haemodialysis
questions.question: Haemodialysis is useful in cases of toxicity by one of the following drugs:

options.A: Drug with Vd = 200 L/ 70 kg B.W.
options.B: Drug with Vd = 10 L/ kg B.W.
options.C: Drug with Vd = 15 L/ 70 kg B.W.
options.D: Drug with Vd = 5 L/ kg B.W.

explanations.A: Incorrect. A Vd of 200 L/70 kg (about 2.9 L/kg) is high, meaning the drug distributes extensively into tissue rather than staying in the vascular compartment a dialysis membrane can access -- haemodialysis is not effective for a drug with such a large Vd.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A Vd of 10 L/kg is enormous, far larger than total body water, meaning almost all of the drug has left the plasma for tissue. Haemodialysis cannot reach a drug distributed this extensively.
explanations.C: Correct. A Vd of 15 L/70 kg (about 0.2 L/kg) is low, close to plasma volume, meaning the drug stays largely confined to the vascular compartment rather than distributing into tissue. Haemodialysis is effective precisely because it can access and remove a drug that remains mostly in the blood.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A Vd of 5 L/kg is very high, meaning the drug is extensively tissue-bound and largely inaccessible to a dialysis membrane that can only clear what remains in the plasma.

questions.subtopic: Volume of distribution and clinical extremes
questions.learning_objective: Apply the principle that haemodialysis works only for drugs with a low volume of distribution close to plasma volume.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Drug with Vd = 15 L/ 70 kg B.W."

questions.title: A drug without extensive first-pass metabolism
questions.question: Extensive first-pass metabolism does not occur with:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Insulin is a peptide destroyed by gastrointestinal and hepatic enzymes if given orally, so it undergoes extensive first-pass-type degradation -- which is exactly why it is never given by the oral route.
explanations.B: Correct. Aminoglycosides are not given orally at all, since they are poorly absorbed from the gut and are instead given parenterally. Because they are not administered by a route that passes through the liver before reaching the systemic circulation, hepatic first-pass metabolism does not meaningfully apply to their usual clinical use.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Lidocaine undergoes extensive hepatic first-pass metabolism, which is exactly why it is not given orally for systemic effect and is instead given intravenously or applied locally to bypass that first pass.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Epinephrine undergoes extensive first-pass metabolism, being rapidly broken down by gut and liver enzymes such as MAO and COMT, which is why it is not given orally for systemic effect.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that a drug never given orally (aminoglycosides) does not meaningfully undergo hepatic first-pass metabolism, unlike drugs whose oral route is specifically avoided because of it.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Aminoglycosides"

questions.title: What does not affect volume of distribution
questions.question: Vd is affected by all the following factors EXCEPT:

options.A: Plasma protein binding of the drug

explanations.A: This DOES affect Vd, so it is not the exception. Plasma protein binding keeps a drug in the vascular compartment, lowering its apparent Vd; a drug that binds tissue proteins more than plasma proteins instead shows a higher Vd.
explanations.B: Correct -- this is the exception. First-pass metabolism determines how much of an orally administered dose reaches the systemic circulation, a separate pharmacokinetic parameter (bioavailability) from Vd. It does not describe how a drug, once in the circulation, distributes between plasma and tissue.
explanations.C: This DOES affect Vd, so it is not the exception. The degree of ionisation at physiological pH affects how readily a drug crosses membranes into tissue, and therefore affects its distribution and Vd.
explanations.D: This DOES affect Vd, so it is not the exception. Lipid solubility determines how readily a drug crosses cell membranes into tissue compartments, directly affecting Vd -- a highly lipid-soluble drug typically has a larger Vd.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish the determinants of Vd (protein binding, ionisation, lipid solubility) from bioavailability determinants such as first-pass metabolism.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: First-pass metabolism"

questions.title: Routes for a drug with low oral bioavailability
questions.question: Drugs with low oral bioavailability are better to be given by all the following routes except:

explanations.A: Correct -- this is the exception. The rectal route still involves partial exposure to hepatic first-pass metabolism, since the upper rectal veins drain into the portal system. Unlike the other three routes listed, it therefore does not reliably avoid the low-bioavailability problem this question is about.
explanations.B: This DOES avoid the low-oral-bioavailability problem, so it is not the exception. The intramuscular route delivers the drug directly into the systemic circulation via muscle capillaries, bypassing the gut and liver first pass entirely.
explanations.C: This DOES avoid the low-oral-bioavailability problem, so it is not the exception. The intravenous route delivers the drug directly into the systemic circulation, bypassing absorption and first-pass metabolism entirely, giving 100% bioavailability by definition.
explanations.D: This DOES avoid the low-oral-bioavailability problem, so it is not the exception. The sublingual route is absorbed directly into the systemic venous drainage of the mouth, bypassing the portal circulation and hepatic first pass entirely.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the rectal route, unlike IM, IV or sublingual, does not reliably avoid hepatic first-pass metabolism.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Rectal"

questions.title: What does not affect bioavailability
questions.question: Bioavailability is affected by all the following factors EXCEPT:

options.B: Plasma protein binding of the drug

explanations.A: This DOES affect bioavailability, so it is not the exception. Food in the gut can alter gastric emptying, gut motility and drug dissolution, changing how much of an oral dose is ultimately absorbed.
explanations.B: Correct -- this is the exception. Plasma protein binding affects a drug once it is already in the systemic circulation, influencing its distribution and free fraction. It does not affect how much of an oral dose reaches that circulation in the first place, so it does not affect bioavailability.
explanations.C: This DOES affect bioavailability, so it is not the exception. Lipid solubility affects how readily a drug crosses the gut wall to be absorbed, directly influencing the fraction of the dose that reaches the systemic circulation.
explanations.D: This DOES affect bioavailability, so it is not the exception. First-pass metabolism removes part of an absorbed oral dose before it reaches the systemic circulation, directly reducing bioavailability by definition.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish bioavailability's determinants (food, lipid solubility, first-pass metabolism) from a distribution parameter, plasma protein binding, that does not affect it.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Plasma protein binding of the drug"

questions.title: Definition of bioavailability
questions.question: The fraction of a given dose that reaches systemic circulation is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Clearance describes the volume of plasma cleared of drug per unit time, a measure of elimination, not the fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Volume of distribution relates the amount of drug in the body to its plasma concentration; it does not describe what fraction of a dose reaches the systemic circulation.
explanations.C: Correct. Bioavailability is defined precisely as the fraction of an administered dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. It is 100% by definition for an intravenous dose, and typically lower for an oral dose because of incomplete absorption and first-pass metabolism.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Half-life is the time for the plasma concentration to fall by half; it describes the rate of elimination, not the fraction of a dose that reaches the systemic circulation.

questions.learning_objective: Define bioavailability as the fraction of an administered dose reaching the systemic circulation, distinct from clearance, Vd and half-life.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: The bioavailability"
field_notes.pendingConcept: CON-FND-CF40F32A8A74A0, same pending Kasr 108-INT concept as Q111 above -- applies only after that batch is live

questions.title: A cause of low oral bioavailability
questions.question: Low oral bioavailability may be due to:

options.A: Extensive metabolism by the digestive enzymes
options.B: High plasma protein binding of the drug
options.C: High lipid solubility of the drug
options.D: Low plasma protein binding of the drug

explanations.A: Correct. Extensive metabolism of a drug by digestive (gut wall) or hepatic first-pass enzymes happens before it reaches the systemic circulation, so it directly reduces the fraction of the oral dose that survives intact. This reduced surviving fraction is exactly what defines low bioavailability.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Plasma protein binding acts on a drug once it has already reached the systemic circulation, not before or during absorption, so it does not explain low oral bioavailability.
explanations.C: Incorrect. High lipid solubility generally favours, rather than impairs, absorption across the gut wall, so it would not by itself explain a low bioavailability -- extensive first-pass/gut-wall metabolism is the more direct cause.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Plasma protein binding, high or low, acts after a drug has already reached the systemic circulation, so it does not explain why less of an oral dose reached that circulation in the first place.

questions.learning_objective: Identify extensive first-pass/gut-wall metabolism as a cause of low oral bioavailability, distinct from plasma protein binding.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Extensive metabolism by the digestive enzymes"

questions.title: A drug with a low volume of distribution
questions.question: Drug with low Vd is:

explanations.A: Correct. Aspirin is highly plasma-protein-bound, which keeps most of it confined to the vascular/extracellular compartment rather than penetrating into tissue. This gives it a low volume of distribution relative to drugs such as digoxin, quinidine and chloroquine, which concentrate heavily in tissue.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Digoxin has a very large volume of distribution because it binds extensively to tissue, particularly skeletal and cardiac muscle, rather than staying in the plasma, so it does not fit the low-Vd description.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Quinidine has a substantial volume of distribution, distributing well beyond the plasma compartment into tissue, unlike a low-Vd drug such as aspirin.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Chloroquine has an extremely large volume of distribution, since it concentrates heavily in tissues such as the liver and spleen, making it one of the classic examples of a very high-Vd drug -- the opposite of what this question asks for.

questions.subtopic: Volume of distribution and clinical extremes

questions.title: A property a clinically used drug may have
questions.question: Clinically used drug may have:

options.B: Vd equal to 3 L/ 70 Kg B.W.

explanations.A: Incorrect. 100% plasma protein binding is not realistic for a drug in ordinary clinical use -- some free (unbound) fraction is always present, since it is the free fraction that produces the pharmacological effect.
explanations.B: Incorrect as the best answer here. A Vd of 3 L/70 kg roughly equals plasma volume, which is not itself impossible, but this quiz's printed key marks the half-life example (option D) as the single correct answer among these four, so it is not the option this question is testing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Bioavailability is a fraction of the administered dose and, by definition, cannot exceed 1 (100%) -- a bioavailability of "2" is a mathematical impossibility, not a real property any drug can have.
explanations.D: Correct. A biological half-life of only a few seconds is physiologically real for some clinically used drugs, such as very rapidly metabolised or redistributed agents. That stands in contrast to the impossible values in the other three options -- 100% protein binding and a bioavailability above 1 -- which no real drug can have.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise a half-life of a few seconds as physiologically possible, and bioavailability above 1 or plasma protein binding of exactly 100% as not.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Biological half-life few seconds"

questions.title: A drug with constant clearance at high dose
questions.question: Constant clearance occurs with high dose of:

explanations.A: Correct. Propranolol is eliminated by ordinary first-order kinetics across its clinical dose range, so its clearance stays constant even at high doses. This is unlike drugs whose elimination pathway becomes saturated, where clearance instead falls as the dose rises.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Phenytoin follows zero-order (saturation) kinetics at doses within or near the therapeutic range -- its metabolising enzyme becomes saturated, so its clearance actually falls, rather than staying constant, as the dose rises.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Ethanol is metabolised by a saturable enzyme (alcohol dehydrogenase) and follows zero-order kinetics at ordinary drinking doses, so a constant amount, not a constant fraction, is eliminated per unit time -- its clearance is not constant at high doses.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Aspirin's elimination becomes saturable at high, toxic doses, so its clearance falls rather than staying constant as the dose rises, unlike propranolol, which remains first-order across its usual dose range.

questions.learning_objective: Identify propranolol as remaining first-order (constant clearance) at high dose, unlike phenytoin, ethanol and aspirin, whose elimination saturates.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: Propranolol"

questions.title: Time to reach steady state given a half-life
questions.question: If t1/2 of a drug is 2 days, the Css is reached after:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Steady state takes about four to five half-lives to be reached; with a 2-day half-life that is roughly 8-10 days, not 5 days.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Twelve hours is far shorter than even a single half-life (2 days = 48 hours) for this drug, let alone the four to five half-lives needed to approach steady state.
explanations.C: Correct. Steady state is reached after approximately four to five half-lives of repeated dosing. With a half-life of 2 days, that is roughly 8-10 days, and 9 days (4.5 half-lives) falls squarely within that expected range.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Two days is only one half-life for this drug, at which point the plasma concentration has covered only about half the distance to steady state, not reached it.

questions.learning_objective: Calculate that steady state is reached after four to five half-lives, applying this to a 2-day half-life drug.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: 9 days"

questions.title: A false statement about a 30-hour half-life drug
questions.question: If the t 1/2 of a drug is 30 hours, one of the followings is false:

options.A: This drug has low Vd and large rate of clearance
options.C: If the drug has constant clearance, it is easy to maintain Css
options.D: The drug is used every 24 h.

explanations.A: Correct -- this is the false statement. Half-life is proportional to Vd and inversely proportional to clearance. A drug with LOW Vd and LARGE clearance would have a SHORT half-life, not the 30-hour half-life stated here, so this combination is inconsistent with the given half-life.
explanations.B: This statement IS consistent with a 30-hour half-life, so it is not the false one. Steady state after four to five half-lives (roughly 120-150 hours, or 5-6 days) is exactly the expected time course for a drug with this half-life.
explanations.C: This statement IS true in general, so it is not the false one. A drug with constant (first-order) clearance produces a predictable, stable steady-state concentration, which is precisely what makes maintaining Css straightforward.
explanations.D: This statement IS a reasonable true dosing choice, so it is not the false one. Giving a drug with a long, 30-hour half-life once daily is a standard, practical dosing interval that keeps fluctuations modest between doses.

questions.learning_objective: Apply the relationship t1/2 proportional to Vd/clearance to recognise that low Vd with large clearance is inconsistent with a stated 30-hour half-life.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: This drug has low Vd and large rate of clearance"

questions.title: Dosing interval given an 18-hour half-life
questions.question: If the T1/2 of a drug is 18 h, it is better to give this drug every:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Dosing only once every 24 hours for a drug with an 18-hour half-life would let the plasma concentration fall considerably between doses, producing larger peak-to-trough swings than a shorter interval.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Dosing every 10 hours is shorter than needed relative to an 18-hour half-life and would risk drug accumulation beyond what is required to maintain a stable therapeutic level.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Dosing every 6 hours is considerably shorter than the drug's half-life and would risk excessive accumulation with repeated dosing.
explanations.D: Correct. A dosing interval close to the drug's own half-life, roughly 12 hours for an 18-hour half-life, is the standard practical choice. It balances convenience against keeping peak-to-trough fluctuations in plasma concentration within a reasonable, manageable range.

questions.learning_objective: Select a dosing interval close to a drug's half-life to balance accumulation against peak-to-trough fluctuation.

field_notes.keySource: printed "The correct answer is: 12 h"

questions.title: When TDM is not indicated
questions.question: TDM is indicated in all the following conditions EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Correct -- this is the exception. Ordinary antihypertensive drugs are typically titrated by clinical response, blood pressure readings, rather than by measuring plasma drug levels. Routine therapeutic drug monitoring is therefore not generally indicated for this drug class as a whole.
explanations.B: This DOES indicate TDM, so it is not the exception. Renal failure alters drug clearance unpredictably for renally-eliminated drugs, making plasma-level monitoring valuable to avoid toxic accumulation.
explanations.C: This DOES indicate TDM, so it is not the exception. Multidrug therapy raises the risk of pharmacokinetic drug-drug interactions that unpredictably alter plasma levels, making monitoring useful to confirm a drug remains in its therapeutic range.
explanations.D: This DOES indicate TDM, so it is not the exception. A narrow therapeutic index means the margin between an effective and a toxic concentration is small, precisely the situation where measuring plasma levels directly is most valuable.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that routine antihypertensive therapy is monitored by clinical response, not TDM, unlike narrow-therapeutic-index drugs, renal failure or multidrug therapy.

questions.title: A drug not monitored by TDM
questions.question: TDM is not indicated in patients using:

explanations.A: This DOES warrant TDM, so it is not the answer. Carbamazepine has a narrow therapeutic index and variable metabolism, both classic indications for therapeutic drug monitoring.
explanations.B: Correct. Insulin's dose is titrated by directly measuring its clinical/biochemical effect, blood glucose, rather than by measuring the plasma insulin concentration itself. Conventional TDM, assaying plasma drug level, is therefore not how insulin therapy is monitored.
explanations.C: This DOES warrant TDM, so it is not the answer. Phenytoin has a narrow therapeutic index and non-linear kinetics near the therapeutic range, both classic indications for therapeutic drug monitoring.
explanations.D: This DOES warrant TDM, so it is not the answer. Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index with a small margin between effective and toxic plasma levels, a classic indication for therapeutic drug monitoring.

questions.title: What does not affect half-life
questions.question: The half-life is affected by all the following factors EXCEPT:

explanations.A: This DOES affect half-life, so it is not the exception. Lipid solubility influences distribution into tissue (Vd), and since half-life depends on Vd, it is affected indirectly through this route.
explanations.B: This DOES affect half-life, so it is not the exception. Plasma protein binding affects both Vd and clearance, both of which determine half-life.
explanations.C: This DOES affect half-life, so it is not the exception. Genetic polymorphisms in metabolising enzymes change clearance, which directly changes half-life.
explanations.D: Correct -- this is the exception. First-pass metabolism determines what fraction of an oral dose reaches the systemic circulation before distribution and elimination even begin. It is not one of the two determinants, Vd and clearance, that together define half-life once the drug is in the body.

questions.learning_objective: Distinguish half-life's true determinants (Vd and clearance, and what changes them) from first-pass metabolism, which acts before distribution and elimination.

questions.title: What the loading dose depends on
questions.question: The loading dose depends on:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Clearance determines the MAINTENANCE dose, the rate needed to replace what is continuously eliminated, not the loading dose.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Half-life determines the dosing INTERVAL and time to steady state, not the size of a loading dose.
explanations.C: Correct. A loading dose is calculated to rapidly achieve a target plasma concentration in the volume the drug will distribute into: loading dose equals Vd multiplied by target concentration. It therefore depends directly on the drug's volume of distribution.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Bioavailability (F) adjusts a dose for the fraction actually reaching the circulation by a given route, but the underlying loading-dose calculation is built on Vd and target concentration, not on F as the primary determinant being tested here.

questions.learning_objective: State that the loading dose is calculated from volume of distribution and target concentration.

questions.title: What the maintenance dose depends on
questions.question: The maintenance dose depends on:

explanations.A: Correct. The maintenance dose replaces exactly what is eliminated between doses, so it is calculated from clearance, the rate of drug removal, and the target steady-state concentration. Maintenance dose rate equals clearance multiplied by target concentration.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Bioavailability adjusts how a given administered dose translates into the amount actually reaching the circulation, but the underlying rate calculation for maintenance dosing is built on clearance, not on F as the primary determinant being tested here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Volume of distribution determines the LOADING dose, the amount needed to rapidly fill that volume to a target concentration, not the ongoing maintenance dose.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Half-life determines dosing interval and time to steady state, not the size of the maintenance dose itself, which is instead set by clearance.

questions.learning_objective: State that the maintenance dose is calculated from clearance, contrasted with the loading dose's dependence on Vd.

questions.title: Plasma concentration after four half-lives
questions.question: We stopped the use of a certain drug when its plasma concentration was 100 mg. What is the plasma concentration of this drug after 20 h if its half-life (t1/2) is 5 h?

explanations.A: Incorrect. 25 mg would be the level after only two half-lives (10 hours), not the four half-lives (20 hours) this question actually asks about.
explanations.B: Incorrect. 12.5 mg would be the level after three half-lives (15 hours), not the full four half-lives, 20 hours, elapsed here.
explanations.C: Correct. Twenty hours divided by a 5-hour half-life is exactly four half-lives, and the plasma concentration halves with each one. So 100 mg falls to 50 mg, then 25 mg, then 12.5 mg, then 6.25 mg after the fourth half-life -- giving 6.25 mg at 20 hours.
explanations.D: Incorrect. 1 mg would require roughly seven half-lives of decline from 100 mg, far more than the four half-lives that have actually elapsed in 20 hours.

questions.learning_objective: Calculate remaining plasma concentration after a given number of elapsed half-lives.
